question: to the Commission Lefteris Nikolaou-Alavanos (NI) Subject:

The residents of Agia Efthymia – a historical village of martyrdom and special cultural significance in the region of Fokida – are opposed to the plan to build a solar farm in a Natura zone in the area. Machinery has already been brought in to clear 170 hectares of forest ahead of construction. The solar farm is being built on both public forest and private land, with landowners seeing their land cleared. Propelled by EU strategies, the Nea Demokratia Government is speeding up the roll-out of wind turbines and photovoltaics, while the policy to phase out lignite has resulted in incalculable consequences. Promises of supposedly cheaper energy are being shattered by the unaffordable cost of ‘green’ energy, while Central Greece has become an energy centre for renewables. At the same time, the ‘war-induced’ price hikes affecting energy and fuel are the other side of the same coin. In the light of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

What is its view regarding the concerns expressed by the residents of Agia Efthymia in Fokida in relation to the construction of a solar farm in the area, despite the Region’s negative opinion, as well as regarding the encroachment on private property?

What view does it take of the fact that the regulation on ‘nature restoration’ has paved the way for even Natura areas to be encroached upon when the interests of energy conglomerates are at stake, under the pretext of being in the ‘overriding public interest’, while in reality the people are paying a high price for the environmental and economic consequences of the unregulated expansion of renewable energy sources?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (6.7.2026) According to Article 6(3) of the Habitats Directive1, projects likely to have a significant impact on Natura 2000 sites must undergo an appropriate assessment and can only proceed if the integrity of the sites is safeguarded. Exceptionally, authorisation may be granted under Article 6(4) if there are imperative reasons of overriding public interest and respective compensatory measures are adopted. According to the revised Renewable Energy Directive2, renewable energy systems are presumed as being in the overriding public interest for the purpose of Article 6(4) of the Habitats Directive. Additionally, the provisions of Article 6(4) including compensatory measures, remain fully applicable. Under the Nature Restoration Regulation3, for the purposes of the derogations from the obligations of continuous improvement and non-deterioration outside Natura 2000 sites, projects for the production of energy from renewable sources are presumed as being of overriding public interest. However, this does not affect the application of the requirements under the Habitats Directive within Natura 2000 sites, where any such project remains subject to the conditions set out in Article 6(4) of the Habitats Directive. Without prejudice to the Commission’s role as guardian of the Treaties, it is primarily the responsibility of the Greek authorities to ensure compliance with EU environmental law.
1 Council Directive 92/43/EEC of 21 May 1992 on the conservation of natural habitats and of wild fauna and

flora, OJ L 206, 22.7.1992, pp. 7–50. 2 Directive (EU) 2023/2413 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 18 October 2023 amending Directive (EU) 2018/2001, Regulation (EU) 2018/1999 and Directive 98/70/EC as regards the promotion of energy from renewable sources, and repealing Council Directive (EU) 2015/652, OJ L, 2023/2413, 31.10.2023. 3 Regulation (EU) 2024/1991 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 24 June 2024 on nature restoration and amending Regulation (EU) 2022/869, OJ L, 2024/1991, 29.7.2024.
